post.description:
Remove ONE tag from a contact in this workspace's connected CRM — 'take the VIP tag off them', 'remove the cold-lead tag'. It removes only the named tag and leaves every other tag untouched. The tag must already exist in this connection's tag registry. Not for adding a tag — that is `ghl.apply_tag`. Over the API it answers in two calls: without confirmation_id it proposes — says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes, spends and sends nothing; the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key, do it.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

contactId.description: The CRM contact id to tag. Required — this never guesses.

tag.description: The ONE tag name to add or remove. Exactly one; there is no bulk form.

confirmation_id.description: Omit to propose: the first call says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes nothing. To go ahead, send the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key; a service account's key can propose but never confirm.

post.description:
Send ONE email to a contact through this workspace's connected CRM, using the CRM's own sending domain — 'email this contact about the offer', 'send them a follow-up email'. It puts a message in a real person's inbox and cannot be recalled, so it PREPARES the send and stops: the operator is shown the subject, the body and who it is going to on a card, and only their approve sends it. Not for this week's marketing campaign email — that is `email_campaign.draft`. Over the API it answers in two calls: without confirmation_id it proposes — says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes, spends and sends nothing; the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key, do it.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

html.description: HTML body. At least one of `html` or `text` is required — a send with neither is refused.

text.description: Plain-text body. At least one of `html` or `text` is required — a send with neither is refused.

fromAddress.description: A VERIFIED sending address on the connected sub-account. Required: there is no default sender to fall back to, and an unverified address is refused by the provider.

confirmation_id.description: Omit to propose: the first call says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes nothing. To go ahead, send the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key; a service account's key can propose but never confirm.

post.description:
Open the member's Splash Pad, the general space where ideas and research start — 'where do I just think out loud?', 'open my scratch space', 'I want somewhere to start this'.  Open the operator's Splash Pad — the general workspace where discovery sessions, drafts, research and ideas start. If they name a pad with board_id, or they are already on one, or the workspace has exactly one, this returns THAT board untouched instead of making a second; otherwise it opens a new one and names the pads they already had. Nothing is published and nothing is spent. Not for renaming a pad — that is `splash_pad.rename`.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

post.description:
Draft an article for the member — 'write me a blog post about this', 'draft an article on that topic', 'put together a write-up for the website'.  Draft an article onto the operator's Splash Pad. Use it when they ask for an article, a blog post, or a written piece for their website. You write the words: pass the headline they asked for and the body as markdown. It creates the draft and hands back a link to the article's workflow, where THEY mark it final, make it a piece and publish it — this tool does none of those and never publishes anything. Not for putting a finished article on a site's blog — that is `page.write_article`.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

title.description: The headline, as the operator would write it. REQUIRED — nothing is derived from the body, because an article published without a real title reads as “(no title)” to readers.

body_markdown.description: The article itself, in markdown. Headings, bold, italic, lists and links are kept; anything else arrives as its text.

post.description:
Write the plan for a funnel — 'plan a funnel for our webinar', 'what would a lead funnel for this offer need?' — what it needs, in what order, where the operator decides, and how each part will be proven. Ask the few questions that matter first (the offer, who it is for, where the traffic comes from, what counts as a conversion, how long the follow-up runs), state a default rather than asking a fifth time, and stop when you have enough. It creates NOTHING: the plan is text they read and change before anything is built. Not for creating the funnel's project once they agree — that is `funnel.scaffold`.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

parameters.description: Your own id for this request, echoed back and recorded on the audit trail. 1–128 characters from `A–Z a–z 0–9 . _ : -`, starting with a letter or digit; anything else is replaced by a generated id.

offer.description: What they are selling, in their own words. Ask for this first — everything else follows from it.

entry_point.description: Where the traffic comes from — ads, organic, cold email, referral. If they have not said, state the default and move on.

conversion_event.description: The one thing that counts as a conversion — a booked call, a purchase, a form fill.

follow_up_window.description: How long the follow-up runs, e.g. 14 days. Default it and say so rather than asking a fifth question they do not care about.

parts.description: Which parts this funnel needs. Choose from the closed list — you cannot invent one. A funnel with a page and a sequence is a real funnel; do not add parts nobody asked for.

defaulted.description: Which of the five answers YOU supplied rather than the operator. The plan marks each one so they can see what they never actually decided. Leave it out when they answered everything.

post.description:
Create the project for a funnel the operator has agreed to — 'yes, set that funnel up', 'build the project for this plan': the project, the plan saved on it as its brief, and one board per part in build order. Nothing else is made — no pages, no emails, no creative. Only call it after they have read the plan and said yes. Not for writing or changing the plan — that is `funnel.plan`.

post.description:
Send a finished campaign board for a person's approval — 'submit this campaign', 'send it for approval'. It creates the pending change and does NOT launch anything: a person approves it in the review queue, and that approval is what launches. Not for checking whether the campaign is ready to go live — that is `ads.launch_check`. Over the API it answers in two calls: without confirmation_id it proposes — says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes, spends and sends nothing; the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key, do it.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

post.description:
Read this brand's fee-transparent ad statement for one month — 'what did we spend on ads last month?', 'show me our ad statement for August' — what they paid each ad platform directly, and what they paid us, as TWO SEPARATE FIGURES. ⚠️ Always report the two separately and NEVER add them together or quote a combined total: the split is a compliance requirement, not a formatting preference, and their ad budget never passes through us. Set produce_if_missing to build a statement for a complete past month that has none yet; that is idempotent and spends nothing. The downloadable copy lives on the Ad statements page. Not for where the account's credits went — that is `billing.usage_summary`.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

post.description:
Check what one competitor is currently running as ads — 'what ads is our competitor running', 'pull up their ads'. Look up what ONE competitor is currently running in the Meta or Google ad library, longest-running first — the ads they keep paying for are the ones working. Costs one lookup, so pull a competitor the operator actually named; a competitor pulled in the last 30 days answers from what we already have and costs nothing unless you set refresh. ⚠️ The ads' image and video files are NOT returned and are never stored — point the operator at each run's Ad Library link when they want to see the creative. Not for suggesting which competitors to watch — that is `ads.suggest_competitors`. Over the API it answers in two calls: without confirmation_id it proposes — says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes, spends and sends nothing; the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key, do it.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

competitor.description: The competitor, in the operator's own words — a brand name. A platform-native page id or advertiser id also works when they have one.

platform.description: Which ad library to look in.

limit.description: How many of their longest-running ads to keep. Defaults to three, which is what the card shows.

refresh.description: Look them up again even though we already have a recent pull saved. This SPENDS a lookup; leave it off unless the operator asked for fresh numbers.

confirmation_id.description: Omit to propose: the first call says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes nothing. To go ahead, send the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key; a service account's key can propose but never confirm.

post.description:
Suggest a few competitors worth tracking — 'who are our competitors', 'suggest some competitors to watch'. Offer TWO OR THREE competitors — never six — for the operator to confirm, guessed from what you know of their brand and site. This does NOT start tracking them and does NOT look anything up: each one is recorded as a candidate waiting for the operator's yes. Give a short honest reason per name; they read it before confirming. Once they confirm, use ads.research_pull to see what that competitor is running. Not for looking up what a named competitor is running — that is `ads.research_pull`.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

Each proposal carries the numbers behind it. Say what it proposed and what it skipped, and say plainly when there is not a full day of data yet or when the outcomes ledger could not be read, rather than reporting a quiet week. Not for changing one campaign's budget or settings directly — that is `ads.save_step`.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

post.description:
Check or save this brand's Google Ads settings — 'what's missing before we can run a campaign', 'save our business phone number for Google Ads'. Read this brand's Google Ads campaign settings — how Google spends the budget, the Smart campaign details, and the Performance Max assets — and save one section of them. Reading changes nothing. ⚠️ These are a real business's name, phone number, landing page and ad copy: NEVER invent any of them, always ask the operator, and read first so you can say exactly what is still missing. Nothing here reaches Google or spends anything; it is what makes a campaign creatable at all. Not for creating the campaign itself — that is `ads.create_smart_campaign` or `ads.create_pmax_campaign`. Over the API it answers in two calls: without confirmation_id it proposes — says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes, spends and sends nothing; the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key, do it.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

parameters.description: Your own id for this request, echoed back and recorded on the audit trail. 1–128 characters from `A–Z a–z 0–9 . _ : -`, starting with a letter or digit; anything else is replaced by a generated id.

section.description: Which section to SAVE. Omit it to only read what is already set — reading changes nothing.

bidding.description: Required when section is `bidding`. ⚠️ A Performance Max campaign only runs on `maximize_conversions` or `maximize_conversion_value`; `target_spend` is search-only and is the default every unconfigured brand has.

smart.description: Required when section is `smart`. These are a REAL business's identity, phone number, landing page and ad copy — never invent any of them; ask the operator. Give the business name OR the Business Profile location, and the landing page URL OR use_ad_optimized_profile — one of each pair, not both.

pmax.description: Required when section is `pmax`. The three image lists take the ids Google gave each picture when it was uploaded to the ad account — never a URL and never image data.

confirmation_id.description: Omit to propose: the first call says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes nothing. To go ahead, send the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key; a service account's key can propose but never confirm.

workspace.description: Which workspace to run in — its slug. Omit to use your default. With more than one reachable workspace and no default, the call is refused and the choices are listed.

Read the connected Pinterest account's boards and which one pins currently publish to. post.description:
Choose the call-to-action button on this brand's Facebook Page — 'change our Facebook Page button to Book Now', 'set the CTA to Shop Now'. Set the call-to-action button on this brand's Facebook Page. This changes what visitors see on the live Page immediately, so read connections.page_cta first and tell the operator what it is changing FROM. The result is re-read from Facebook, so report what it says rather than what you asked for — Facebook can normalise or refuse part of a request. Not for removing the button altogether — that is `connections.clear_page_cta`.

type.description: The button label, as one of Facebook's exact values — e.g. BOOK_NOW, CALL_NOW, SHOP_NOW, SIGN_UP, LEARN_MORE, CONTACT_US, REQUEST_QUOTE, GET_DIRECTIONS. Not every Page can run every button; if Facebook refuses one, say so and offer a different one rather than retrying the same value.

web_destination_type.description: Where the button sends people, as one of Facebook's exact values — WEBSITE for a link, EMAIL for an address, NONE for a button with no destination. Leave it out for a plain website or phone button: it is derived from what you supply. Required for an EMAIL button.

web_url.description: The full https link the button opens. Required for a button that sends people to a website; leave it out for CALL_NOW.

phone_number.description: For CALL_NOW: the number in full international form, starting with + (e.g. +14155550123). A national-format number dials wrong for half the callers and is refused.

email_address.description: For an email-destination button: the address to open.

Remove the call-to-action button from this brand's Facebook Page entirely. Re-read one of this workspace's own connectors' tool list right now — 'refresh our custom connector', 'why aren't the new tools showing up'. Re-read one of this workspace's own registered connectors' tool list, right now. Use it when the operator says they have added or changed something on their own MCP server or API and the new operations are not showing up — this asks the connector again, where the connector card reports the LAST sync. post.description:
Turn one of this Page's published posts into a boosted ad — 'boost this post', 'turn this post into an ad'. Boost one published Facebook Page post into an ad for that Page. Before it runs, the member is shown the post, the daily budget and the days on a card and approves it there. It does NOT start spending: the ad account's own spend approval still stands in front of any money, and everything it creates is PAUSED. Report the status field exactly as returned — never say the ad is live or running. Not for a full campaign built from a brief — that is `ads.apply_brief`. Over the API it answers in two calls: without confirmation_id it proposes — says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes, spends and sends nothing; the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key, do it.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

post.description:
Re-check which accounts a connection can post to, and record what the provider answers — 'my page isn't showing up as somewhere to post', 'I just connected Instagram, why can't I pick it?', 'check my accounts again'.  Re-read one connection for the accounts this brand can post to, and record them. Use it when the operator says a connected account is not showing up as somewhere to post, or right after they connect one. It only asks the provider: nothing is published, no setting changes, no credential is read or returned — and it never picks WHICH account is this brand's, it reports when that question is open. post.description:
Confirm we actually have access to a brand's shared ad account — 'check if the ad account access came through', 'did they finish sharing the ad account'. Ask the platform what access we ACTUALLY have on this brand's ad account right now, and record the answer. Call it when the operator says they have finished sharing the account, or asks whether it came through. It needs their ad account id already on file — connections.ad_account_status shows whether we have one. On TikTok this is what catches the common failure: TikTok's default sharing level is view-only, so a shared account often arrives with access that cannot run campaigns, and this check surfaces the step that fixes it. It only LOOKS: nothing is changed on their ad account, nothing is spent, and the only thing written is our own record of what came back — so it is always safe to run again. Not for asking the platform for access — that is `connections.request_ad_account_access`.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

Ask the platform for permission to work on the operator's OWN ad account, naming the account id they gave you. This sends a real request that lands in their own business settings for approval, so pass the account id the operator gave you, never one you guessed. It requires a signed authorization to act on their behalf; calling it raises the approval card naming the account and the platform, which is the operator's confirmation, and only their approve sends it. It never moves money and never touches their card. Not for checking access we already asked for — that is `connections.check_ad_account_access`. post.description:
Turn an accepted campaign plan into finished ads — 'draw the ads for this campaign', 'generate the creative now'. Draw this campaign's ads from the plan it already accepted — a picture and its words for each idea. It STARTS the drawing and returns; the drawing carries on by itself even if they close the page, and the pictures land over the next few minutes. It costs money and only works once per campaign. Not for more ads like one that already exists (`ads.more_like_this`) or for pictures that never drew (`ads.retry_draft_pictures`). Over the API it answers in two calls: without confirmation_id it proposes — says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes, spends and sends nothing; the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key, do it.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

post.description:
Prove ONE configured part of a funnel — 'test the landing page', 'check the first email sends' — by running a synthetic test lead through it — a form fill that has to land a lead, a first send that has to reach the test inbox. The lead is always synthetic and every send goes to the workspace's designated test address, never a real person. It writes `passed`, or `failed` naming the exact step, onto the funnel's plan. A part that has not passed is unverified, never done — and the funnel AS A WHOLE stays unverified however many parts pass. Not for the whole funnel end to end — that is `funnel.test_end_to_end`. Over the API it answers in two calls: without confirmation_id it proposes — says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes, spends and sends nothing; the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key, do it.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

post.description:
Push one local post out to this workspace's Google Business Profile — 'post this update to our Google Business Profile', 'publish a local post about our sale'. Publish one local post to this workspace's Google Business Profile. It is PUBLIC — customers see it on the business's listing — so calling it raises the approval card showing the exact wording, which is the operator's confirmation, and only their approve publishes it. Check `connections.business_profile_status` first and do not offer this when `can_publish` is false. The text goes out exactly as written. Not for whether a local post can go out right now — that is `connections.business_profile_status`. Over the API it answers in two calls: without confirmation_id it proposes — says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes, spends and sends nothing; the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key, do it.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

parameters.name: x-request-id
parameters.description: Your own id for this request, echoed back and recorded on the audit trail. 1–128 characters from `A–Z a–z 0–9 . _ : -`, starting with a letter or digit; anything else is replaced by a generated id.

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key
parameters.description: Your key for this write: send the same key when you retry and the first result comes back instead of a second action. Keys are honoured for at least 24 hours. 1–200 visible ASCII characters. Replaces the `idempotency_key` body field, which still works until 2026-12-31; this action needs a key on one of the two, and the header is the one to send.

piece_id.description: The content piece this post came from. It is what makes the published post reconcilable back to what the operator approved — never invent one, and never reuse another piece's id.

text.description: The post body, exactly as the operator approved it. On a Business Profile the text IS the post — there is no caption/body split — so do not append hashtags, links or sign-offs the operator did not write.

media_url.description: One photo or video URL, or null for a text-only post. A Business Profile local post carries at most ONE media item; a second is refused rather than dropped.

media_type.description: What `media_url` points at. Null when there is no media. Must match the asset — a mislabelled type is refused by Google, not silently corrected.

media_mime_type.description: The asset's MIME type, e.g. `image/jpeg` or `video/mp4`. Null when there is no media. Read it off the asset — never guess one to satisfy the field.

idempotency_key.description: Deprecated on REST: send the `Idempotency-Key` header instead. Still accepted until 2026-12-31; if both are sent they must match.

confirmation_id.description: Omit to propose: the first call says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes nothing. To go ahead, send the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key; a service account's key can propose but never confirm.

workspace.description: Which workspace to run in — its slug. Omit to use your default. With more than one reachable workspace and no default, the call is refused and the choices are listed.

post.description:
Create the measurement a Google Ads campaign optimises toward — 'set up a conversion action', 'add a conversion goal for Performance Max'. Create a Google Ads conversion action for this brand — the measurement a campaign optimises toward — and report what Google read back afterwards. It spends nothing: it creates no budget and attaches to no campaign. A Performance Max campaign needs one before it can bid. Reuse the same idempotency_key on a retry so a retry cannot create a second one. Not for choosing which Google Analytics conversions the brand reports — that is `connections.set_conversion_events`. Over the API it answers in two calls: without confirmation_id it proposes — says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes, spends and sends nothing; the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key, do it.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

Make a spreadsheet — 'put this in a spreadsheet', 'give me an Excel file of that', 'export these as a CSV I can open'.  Create a spreadsheet — an .xlsx workbook or a single-sheet CSV — from data you already have, and save it to this workspace's library. Declare the columns, then give the rows as objects keyed by those columns. On success: tell the operator the file is saved to their library, name it, and give them the download link — say the link is temporary while the file itself stays in the library. Never paste the file's contents back into the conversation. If the result carries `warnings`, the file WAS made but something in it needs saying — read each warning out before you offer the link, and offer to fix what it names. Not for a Data table that lives on a board — that is `data.create_table`.

Create an email template from one of the starter templates. Use a starter key the templates surface offered — never invent one; the server refuses anything it does not recognise. Not for a new sequence of emails — that is `email_sequence.create`.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

post.description:
Hand a finished sequence over to the member's connected marketing tool to send — 'push this into my CRM', 'send it over to my email tool', 'load this sequence into GHL'.  Hand a finished sequence to the customer's connected marketing tool, which then owns the sending. This writes into an outside system, so calling it raises the approval card, which is the operator's confirmation; call it on the ask, and it hands the sequence over only once they approve. It does not send email itself. Not for recording that they copied it out by hand — that is `email_seed.record_export`. Over the API it answers in two calls: without confirmation_id it proposes — says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes, spends and sends nothing; the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key, do it.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

board_id.description: The finished sequence to hand off.

mode_key.description: Which hand-off ending the operator chose. Use a key the seed sheet offered — the server resolves it against its own catalogue and refuses anything else.

audience_key.description: The connected tool's audience/list key, or null when the chosen ending needs none. It is re-read from the provider, never trusted.

start_date.description: The first send date as YYYY-MM-DD, or null when the ending needs none.

confirmation_id.description: Omit to propose: the first call says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes nothing. To go ahead, send the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key; a service account's key can propose but never confirm.

post.description:
List the work waiting on a human right now — 'what's waiting on me?', 'what needs approving?' — rendered and in-review assets, what each one belongs to, and whose desk it is parked on ('you' or 'client'). Each row also carries its videoUnitId and contentBlockId, which is where approvals.request_review's subjectId comes from. Read-only. You can read what is waiting, get an item ready, and ASK a person to decide. You can never approve, reject, or decide anything yourself — say who it is waiting on and stop there. Not for one waiting item in full — that is `approvals.get_item`.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

post.description:
Pick which version of something goes forward — 'use that thumbnail', 'this is the one I want', 'make that the main version'.  Choose which variant of an asset (typically a thumbnail) is the one that goes forward for review. This is CURATION BEFORE approval — it does not approve anything and does not release anything; a person still decides. You can read what is waiting, get an item ready, and ASK a person to decide. You can never approve, reject, or decide anything yourself — say who it is waiting on and stop there. Not for asking someone to approve it — that is `approvals.request_review`.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

post.description: Read the account's own monthly budget and how much of it is spent, and every other spend cap's burn — 'how much of our budget have we used?', 'what's our monthly budget?', 'do we pause at the budget?', 'how close are we to our spend cap?'. `payer_budget` is the budget the account set for itself, in credits: this month's spend against it, whether reaching it emails the owners and admins (`notify`) or pauses work that needs credits (`pause`), and the percentages they are emailed at. Say the figures back exactly as given. If `payer_budget.unavailable` is true, say the budget could not be read; never report that as 'no budget', and never report an unavailable cap list as 'no limits'. The other caps are read-only here. Not for changing the budget — that is `billing.budget_set`; not for the credit balance — that is `billing.plan_status`.

post.description:
Say what ONE thing waiting for a decision actually is — 'what am I approving here?', 'what's this one?', 'why is this waiting on me?'.  Read ONE thing waiting for a decision, by its id ('<kind>:<sourceId>') — what it is, what it says, whether this person can decide it, how long it has waited, and whether a reviewer already has it open. Works for every kind in the review queue, not just assets. Use it for the item on the screen the person is looking at. Check 'status': 'found' means the item is described; 'not_in_queue' means it is decided already or was never theirs; 'source_unavailable' means the read FAILED and nothing is known about it — say so and offer to try again, never say it was decided. Read-only. You can read what is waiting, get an item ready, and ASK a person to decide. You can never approve, reject, or decide anything yourself — say who it is waiting on and stop there. Not for the whole queue of waiting work — that is `approvals.list_queue`.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

Write a reply to someone who wrote in — 'draft a reply to that message', 'write something back to them', 'answer this one for me'.  Write a fresh AI reply for one inbox conversation, using the account's response instructions and the thread so far. The reply lands in the reviews queue for a human to approve, edit or discard — this tool NEVER sends anything. Not for sending a reply that is already waiting — that is `inbox.approve_and_send`. post.description:
Change an email template without changing any email that wears it — 'make the header darker', 'swap the footer on the newsletter template', 'change the template's subject line'. It saves into the template's draft, opening one from the version emails send now when none is open; every email wearing the template keeps sending its current version until the draft is finalized. Leave a field out to keep it as it stands. Read the template with `email_template.list_versions` first for its id, its design and the open draft's revision, and pass that revision back. Not for applying the change to the emails that wear it — that is `email_template.finalize_and_apply`.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

parameters.description: Your own id for this request, echoed back and recorded on the audit trail. 1–128 characters from `A–Z a–z 0–9 . _ : -`, starting with a letter or digit; anything else is replaced by a generated id.

template_id.description: The email template, as `email_template.list_versions` or `email_template.create` named it.

mjml_source.description: The template's whole design as MJML. Leave it out to keep the design as it stands and change only the subject or regions.

subject.description: The template's own subject line. Leave it out to keep it; null clears it.

content.description: The editor's region overrides as one JSON object. Leave it out to keep them; null clears them.

expected_revision.description: The open draft's revision as `email_template.list_versions` or the last save reported it. Leave it out only when no draft is open.

workspace.description: Which workspace to run in — its slug. Omit to use your default. With more than one reachable workspace and no default, the call is refused and the choices are listed.

post.description:
Make a template's draft the version every email wearing it sends — 'apply the new template', 'finalize the template', 'put the new template on my emails'. This changes what real contacts receive from that moment on, so calling it raises the approval card, which shows the final emails and active automations that wear the template and is the member's confirmation; call it on the ask. The version emails sent before stays in the history and can be restored. Not for saving changes — that is `email_template.save_draft`. Over the API it answers in two calls: without confirmation_id it proposes — says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes, spends and sends nothing; the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key, do it.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

post.description:
Bring back an earlier version of a template as a new draft — 'go back to last week's template', 'restore version 2 of the newsletter template'. It opens a draft whose design is that version's; history is never rewritten, and nothing changes for any email until the draft is finalized with `email_template.finalize_and_apply`. It is refused while another draft is open. Not for throwing a draft away — that is `email_template.discard_draft`.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

post.description:
Hide a comment on the brand's public post, or put it back — 'hide that comment', 'take that comment down', 'unhide the one I hid'.  Hide a comment from the brand's public Facebook or Instagram post, or unhide one. Hiding is REVERSIBLE and is what to reach for when a comment should come down — prefer it over inbox.delete_comment, which cannot be undone. The commenter is not told, and nothing is sent to them. Not for deleting the comment for good — that is `inbox.delete_comment`. Over the API it answers in two calls: without confirmation_id it proposes — says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes, spends and sends nothing; the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key, do it.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

hidden.description: true hides the comment from the public post; false unhides it.

confirmation_id.description: Omit to propose: the first call says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes nothing. To go ahead, send the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key; a service account's key can propose but never confirm.

workspace.description: Which workspace to run in — its slug. Omit to use your default. With more than one reachable workspace and no default, the call is refused and the choices are listed.

post.description:
Draft this week's email campaign — 'write this week's email', 'draft the newsletter', 'put together an email about the new offer'.  Draft this week's email campaign from the operator's brief. It creates a DRAFT in the Emails board and sends nothing to anyone — say that plainly, and never imply the campaign has gone out. Ask for the brief rather than inventing one. Calling it raises the approval card, which is the operator's confirmation, so call it on the ask; it drafts once they approve. Not for a multi-email sequence — that is `email_sequence.create`. Over the API it answers in two calls: without confirmation_id it proposes — says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes, spends and sends nothing; the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key, do it.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

post.description:
Answer 'am I in the AI answer for this?' — for each search, whether Google wrote an AI Overview, whether this workspace's site is cited in it, which of our URLs it used, WHO ELSE it cited, where we rank organically on the same page, and whether we hold the featured snippet. Omit `domain` to use this workspace's own site. EACH SEARCH IS A SEPARATE PAID READ and charges credits, so pass only the searches the operator named — at most 5. `ai_overview_present: true` with `ai_overview_resolved: false` means there IS an overview and it could not be read: say that, never 'you are not cited'. `rows` may be SHORTER than the searches you asked about: when `queries_not_read` is non-empty the provider failed part-way, so name each of those searches as one you COULD NOT CHECK — never report them as not cited, and say only `queries_answered` of `queries_requested` were read. Not for the whole results page broken down — that is `seo.serp_features`. Over the API it answers in two calls: without confirmation_id it proposes — says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes, spends and sends nothing; the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key, do it.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

post.description:
Answer 'how strong is this site's link authority?' — how many sites link to it, how many referring domains and pages, its authority rank, its spam score, how many links are broken, and the composition of the profile (link types, nofollow share, top TLDs and countries). This calls a paid provider and CHARGES the workspace credits at a FLAT rate PER REQUEST — the same charge whether a profile is found or not — so use the exact domain the operator named rather than guessing. `has_profile: false` means the index has never seen that EXACT target: say so and name the target you looked up, because a typo produces the same answer as a genuinely unlinked site — never report it as 'your site has no backlinks' without naming what was checked. Over the API it answers in two calls: without confirmation_id it proposes — says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes, spends and sends nothing; the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key, do it.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

post.description:
Audit one live page for SEO issues — 'audit our pricing page', 'what's wrong with this page's SEO'. Audit ONE live page: its title and description with their lengths, every H1, the canonical, whether it is served over HTTPS, whether it carries structured data and whether that data has errors, word count, internal and external link counts, load time, page size, and a list of what is wrong — critical issues first, then warnings. This calls a paid provider and CHARGES the workspace credits per page, so audit the page the operator named rather than crawling around it. `url` in the result is the page ACTUALLY audited and may differ from the one asked for when it redirected — if it does, say so. An empty `issues` list means the checks that were run all passed, not that the page is perfect. Not for the site's link authority — that is `seo.backlinks_summary`. post.description:
Drive a real browser to a page on a site this workspace has APPROVED for browsing and pull named fields off it — 'use the browser to pull the prices off our supplier's page', 'open our approved site in the browser and read the plan table'. Open a web page this workspace has approved for browsing and READ it — pull named fields off it, or answer a question about what is on it. This one is for the approved sites that need a real browser. It only reaches sites the workspace has added on Settings → Assistant → Browser; anything else is refused with the domain to add. It reads and never types, clicks through a form, signs in, or changes anything on the page. Not for an ordinary link someone pastes, or any site to just read — that is `web.read`. Over the API it answers in two calls: without confirmation_id it proposes — says what would happen, returns a confirmation_id and changes, spends and sends nothing; the same arguments again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key, do it.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

post.description:
'set up a posting rhythm', 'we post three times a week' — create one cadence template in this workspace: the weekly rhythm the schedule plans slots from, written out slot by slot (weekday, time, destination, asset type and piece format). Nothing publishes and nothing is scheduled by it. Leave the slots out to create an empty rhythm. Not for making a rhythm the default — that is `cadence_template.set_default`.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

parameters.name: x-request-id
parameters.description: Your own id for this request, echoed back and recorded on the audit trail. 1–128 characters from `A–Z a–z 0–9 . _ : -`, starting with a letter or digit; anything else is replaced by a generated id.

name.description: What to call the rhythm. It must be unique in the workspace — a duplicate is refused, not silently renamed.

description.description: A sentence on what this rhythm is for.

day_of_week.description: Which weekday this slot publishes on, 0 = Monday through 6 = Sunday.

time_of_day.description: The wall-clock time this slot publishes at, HH:MM (24-hour). It is workspace-local, not UTC.

destination.description: Where this slot publishes — the destination key.

required_asset_type.description: What kind of asset this slot expects.

piece_format.description: What kind of content this slot publishes. Required — a slot with no format is invisible to every rhythm view, so the rhythm would run and plan nothing. Pick the one the member described: posts for a social post, stories for a story, shorts_clips for a short vertical video, long_form for a full-length video, articles for a written article, podcast for an audio episode.

approval_required.description: Whether a person must approve before this slot publishes.

items.description: One weekly slot in the rhythm.

slots.description: The weekly slots, in the order they should appear. Leave it out to create an empty rhythm the operator fills in on the Cadence surface.

workspace.description: Which workspace to run in — its slug. Omit to use your default. With more than one reachable workspace and no default, the call is refused and the choices are listed.

post.description:
'retire that rhythm', 'we're not using that pattern any more' — retire one of this workspace's cadence templates, named by its template_id, so it stops being offered for new weeks. It is not deleted: weeks already built from it keep working. It answers in two calls: without confirmation_id it proposes, says what would change and changes nothing; the same call again with that confirmation_id, on a member's own API key, retires it. Not for switching the default rhythm — that is `cadence_template.set_default`.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

post.description:
'how many visitors did we get last week?', 'what's our conversion rate?' — read this workspace's analytics numbers over a window: the same figures, from the same reads, the analytics pages show. Name dictionary keys (analytics.list_available_metrics lists them) and a preset period or an explicit from/to; set compare to also read the preceding window. Every row carries a state: empty is a final answer, read_failed means nothing is known, and suppressed means a small-count privacy floor withholds the figure. It changes nothing. Not for which metrics exist or report here — that is `analytics.list_available_metrics`.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

parameters.name: x-request-id
parameters.description: Your own id for this request, echoed back and recorded on the audit trail. 1–128 characters from `A–Z a–z 0–9 . _ : -`, starting with a letter or digit; anything else is replaced by a generated id.

metric_keys.description: Dictionary metric keys to read. Use analytics.list_available_metrics to discover them.

period.description: A preset window of whole COMPLETE periods ending at the start of the current one: 7d = the last 7 complete days (today is excluded), 28d = the last 4 complete weeks, 90d = the last 3 complete calendar months (92 days on a May-Aug read, not 90). Omit when supplying from/to.

from.description: Window start, ISO-8601 date or timestamp. Inclusive. Requires `to`.

to.description: Window end, ISO-8601 date or timestamp. EXCLUSIVE.

grain.description: Granularity the stored rows are read at. LEAVE THIS UNSET unless you have a specific reason: day is where the analytics store is written, and asking for a coarser grain reads a different set of rows that is usually empty. A window is summed from day rows regardless of how long it is, so a month-long window does NOT need grain=month.

compare.description: Also read the immediately preceding window of the same number of COMPLETE periods, for a like-for-like comparison. On a preset that is a calendar step, so the preceding window holds the same number of weeks or months — not necessarily the same number of days.

by.description: Split each ad sum (ads_spend, ads_impressions, ads_clicks, ads_conversions) by ad platform — Meta, Google, LinkedIn, TikTok, Snapchat — each with its state: measured (a figure), quiet (connected, nothing ran), unread (we do not read that platform's spend yet) or not_connected. A platform with no figure is never a zero. Other keys come back unsplit.

post.description:
'how is our LinkedIn page doing?', 'who follows us on LinkedIn?' — read this workspace's LinkedIn company-page statistics over the grant the workspace connected: followers and their demographics, page views and clicks, and organic post engagement, optionally over a window of days. The answer names the source it read; when LinkedIn is reached only through the workspace's CRM connection it says so and returns no LinkedIn figures. It changes nothing. Not for the cross-platform social totals — that is `analytics.query_metrics`.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

parameters.name: x-request-id
parameters.description: Your own id for this request, echoed back and recorded on the audit trail. 1–128 characters from `A–Z a–z 0–9 . _ : -`, starting with a letter or digit; anything else is replaced by a generated id.

organization_urn.description: The company page to read, as its LinkedIn page URN — the urn:li:… identifier carried on the connected grant. Omit when the connection administers exactly one page — it is then chosen automatically. If several are administered, this is required and the answer lists them.

days.description: Read a trailing window of this many days instead of lifetime totals. OMIT for the lifetime read, which is the only one that carries follower DEMOGRAPHICS (industry, seniority, function, geography) — LinkedIn drops every demographic facet from a time-bound follower query, so a window and a breakdown are two different questions.

include.description: Which sections to read: followers (count + demographics or gains), page_views (views and custom-button clicks), shares (organic impressions, clicks, reactions, comments, engagement rate). Omit for all three. Each section is a separate LinkedIn call, so narrowing this spends less of the page's rate budget.

workspace.description: Which workspace to run in — its slug. Omit to use your default. With more than one reachable workspace and no default, the call is refused and the choices are listed.

200.description: The call was admitted and dispatched. `ok` says whether the tool succeeded — a refusal the tool itself produced is still a 200, exactly as it is a successful JSON-RPC result over MCP.

x-goosy-tool-error.description: `true` when a boundary step refused the call — workspace resolution failed or could not be read. A tool that ran and returned its own typed `ok: false` reports `false` here. **Branch on `ok` in the body for the outcome; this header is the transport-level hint.**

source.description: Which rail these numbers came from. linkedin_cmapi = LinkedIn's own page analytics; ghl = the workspace posts through GoHighLevel, which reports no LinkedIn-specific numbers; none = neither is connected.

provenance.description: The trust class, on the metric dictionary's own axis. Both connected rails are platform_reported — the platform's number, subject to the platform's methodology. Null when there is no number.

source_note.description: The plain-language sentence to tell the operator about where these numbers come from. Say it — never paraphrase it into a stronger claim.

connect_path.description: Where the operator connects LinkedIn page analytics directly, when that would change the answer. Null when already connected on the direct rail.

read_elsewhere.description: On the ghl source ONLY: the cross-platform social metric keys LinkedIn activity is counted inside, and the tool/page that reads them. There is no LinkedIn breakdown to give — offer these instead of guessing one.

organization_urn.description: The company page these numbers are for. Null on the ghl and none sources, which have no page-level read.

administered_organizations.description: Every company page this connection may read. More than one and organization_urn is required.

kind.description: lifetime = no time restriction, and the ONLY kind that carries follower demographics. time_bound = a trailing window.

days.description: The window length asked for. Null on a lifetime read.

granularity.description: The interval each row covers. Null on a lifetime read. LinkedIn's page statistics accept DAY or MONTH only.

follower_window_ends_days_ago.description: LinkedIn publishes time-bound follower data only up to this many days before today, so the follower series legitimately stops short of the rest of the window. Null when no follower series was read.

follower_start_ms.description: The ACTUAL start of the follower interval sent to LinkedIn, epoch ms. Report this rather than inferring it from `days` — the two differ whenever the publication lag applies.

follower_end_ms.description: The ACTUAL end of the follower interval sent to LinkedIn, epoch ms. Null when no follower series was read.

window.description: What was ACTUALLY read — not what was asked for. The two differ whenever LinkedIn's follower publication lag applies.

total_followers.description: The page's total follower count, from LinkedIn's networkSizes read. It is a SEPARATE call from the follower statistics and carries no publication lag. Null when the followers section was not read or its call failed.

key.description: The facet value — a LinkedIn URN or enum, e.g. urn:li:industry:4.

follower_count.description: Organic AND paid followers in this bucket, rolled together.

total_buckets.description: How many buckets LinkedIn returned for this facet in total.

truncated.description: True when buckets is a SUBSET. Never describe a truncated facet as the complete breakdown.

post.description:
Put a video on a page so the page can play it — 'add my product video to the landing page', 'use the new render on this site'. Name one of the workspace's videos, or a finished render to connect it first; a render still being copied answers copying, and the same call made again attaches it. Attaching a video that is not yet hosted starts hosting it, which charges the workspace for encoding, and captions are charged only when named. On a key with no member behind it the first call returns a confirmation id and the second, carrying it back, attaches. Not for taking a video off — that is `page.api_video_detach`.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

post.description:
Take a video off a page — 'remove the old video from the landing page', 'stop this site playing that clip'. It refuses by name while the live version of the page still plays the video, so remove it from the page and publish first. When no page plays the video any more its hosting ends after a grace window and the original stays in the workspace. On a key with no member behind it the first call returns a confirmation id and the second, carrying it back, detaches. Not for putting a video on — that is `page.api_video_attach`.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

post.description:
Bring a video file of the customer's own into the workspace so a page can play it — 'upload our demo video', 'port this mp4 to the site'. Start with the file's name, type and size; the answer is one upload address, or parts to request with sign_parts and send in order; complete records the video, and abort abandons it. The video is stored and never hosted until it is attached to a page; storage is charged per month. On a key with no member behind it, start returns a confirmation_id first, and so does a complete that names captions, because captions are charged per language minute; calling the same action again with that confirmation_id runs the recorded request, and a confirmed complete stores exactly the caption languages it recorded. Not for putting the finished video on a page — that is `page.api_video_attach`.

Every result names the workspace it ran in. Say which workspace the answer is about. When the account has more than one workspace and none is selected, this tool refuses with `workspace_ambiguous` and lists the choices — offer them, never pick one.

post.summary: Import or replace a site from an archive
post.description:
Uploads one ZIP archive and either creates a site or replaces the code of an existing one. The service classifies the archive from its CONTENTS — a prebuilt bundle is staged immediately, a supported source project is queued for the build rail — and validates any `pages.deploy.json` it carries against the published `PagesDeployManifest` schema, returning the manifest it resolved on every success. The archive must be no larger than 41943040 bytes.

**A push onto a site that already holds a code project shows the diff first.** With `siteId` set and a current project on that site, the call answers `202` with `data.outcome: "pending_confirmation"`, the diff against the current project and a `handle` — nothing is written. Send the SAME archive again with `?confirm=<handle>` to apply it (`200`, `outcome: "ingested"`). Byte-identical bytes answer `200` with `outcome: "unchanged"` and write nothing — and where the site's stored source had no build that came up, that same answer carries a `buildRunId`, because re-pushing an unbuilt project queues its build rather than leaving the site dark. Once such a project has spent the rail's build attempts, the answer stays `200` `unchanged` and carries `buildBlocked` instead: re-pushing an identical archive is never an error, so an idempotent deploy stays green, and the field is where a person is told that only a changed file will build. A first upload proceeds directly. The replaced set is the code project only: the site's database, its storage, its media and its data tables are never touched by a push.

parameters.name: workspace
parameters.description: Which workspace to act in — its slug or id. The SAME argument every workspace-scoped tool takes, resolved the same way: an account-wide key may select any workspace its holder currently reaches, a workspace-pinned key may only name its own, and a call that names nothing falls through to your default. It is a QUERY parameter rather than a body field on purpose: this endpoint's body is a multipart upload, and reading a field out of it would decode that body before the bearer and the rate limiter had run. With more than one reachable workspace and no default, the call is refused as `workspace_ambiguous` and the choices are listed. Ignored for a signed-in session, whose workspace comes from its own claims.

parameters.description: The `handle` a previous `202` answered with. Present ⇒ apply the diff that handle was issued for: the archive must be byte-identical to the one the diff was shown for, and the site's current project must still be the base it was shown against, else `400` (`confirmation_stale`). Ignored on a first upload.

post.summary: Dry-run an archive against every import screen
post.description: Runs the SAME screens `ingestPageArchive` runs — the manifest schema, the archive and path guards, the dependency allowlist, recipe resolution, the conformance gate and every declared ceiling — over the archive you send, and answers the FULL list of refusals at once. It spends no build, mints no revision and writes nothing: no site is created or modified, and sending the same archive to the import afterwards is what actually imports it. Read `screensRun` before treating an empty `refusals` as a guarantee: anything we cannot decide without compiling your project stays a build result. Authenticated exactly like the import, and metered as a read.

get.summary: Download a site's code project as a zip
get.description: Streams the site's code project as the zip it would build from: a site you brought as a finished bundle gives back its newest staged revision (the platform's own `bundle.json` left out and its migration relocation undone, so the zip re-imports as it is); a site built here gives back its current source tree. The bytes are built on the way out and never stored, auth is re-checked on every call, and the zip is deterministic for a given revision. `X-Goosy-Export-Ref` names the revision or source ref the zip is byte-identical to. The site's database, storage, media and data tables are not part of the code project and are not in the zip. Pulling a site's code is recorded on the audit ledger and is not metered.

retry_after_seconds.description: On a 429: whole seconds to wait. Mirrors `Retry-After`.

error.description: Deprecated: the same values as the top-level fields, kept until 2026-12-31. Read `code` and `message` at the top level.

Error.description: A request the boundary refused before dispatching anything. The same shape the MCP endpoint answers its own refusals with, and the same top-level fields a dispatched call's refusal carries, so one client branch covers both.

code.description: The typed reason — e.g. `workspace_ambiguous`, `invalid_arguments`, or the tool's own failure code.

message.description: A sentence a person can act on.

workspaces.description: On a workspace refusal: the slugs this key may pass as `workspace`.

issues.description: On `invalid_arguments`: which fields failed, and why.

ToolRefusal.description: A call that was admitted and dispatched, and did not succeed.

PagePreviewLinkError.description: A Pages preview-link request that did not succeed.

PageAssetError.description: A Pages asset upload that did not succeed.

PageIngestError.description: A Pages import that did not succeed. ⚠️ Unlike a tool refusal, this envelope has NO `workspaces` array — on `workspace_ambiguous` and `workspace_unreachable` the slugs you may pass are appended to `error.message` instead.

entry.description: The Worker module that answers `routes`, relative to the bundle root. Omit it for a static site.

assets.description: The directory holding the site's static files, relative to the bundle root.

pattern.description: A site-root-relative path the Worker answers. `*` is allowed only as a trailing `/*`.

access.description: Who may reach this route. `members` requires a member of this site's workspace, signed in to Goosy; the platform enforces it before your code runs. Defaults to `public`.

routes.description: Which paths the Worker answers; everything else is served as a static file. A route whose `access` is `members` is gated by the platform before anything answers it, so a static site with no `entry` may declare members routes and nothing else.

migrations.description: Directory of `.sql` migrations for this site's own database, applied in filename order.

tables.description: The tables this site's code owns.

stagedMigrationsPrefix.description: PLATFORM-WRITTEN. Where the migrations above were actually staged, once the bundle was relocated into the reserved prefix. Never write this yourself — a manifest that carries it on upload is refused.

database.description: The site's own database. Declaring it provisions one on the first build.

projectDatabase.description: How this site reaches the PROJECT database shared by its project's sites. Defaults to `none`.

secrets.description: Secret NAMES this Worker reads. Values are set on the site, never in this file.

submissions.description: A table that platform form posts are also written to, so a static site keeps its own entries.

name.description: The identifier your Worker reads the bucket through. Defaults to `BUCKET`.

storage.description: The site's own object store. Declaring it provisions one bucket on the first publish and binds it.

images.description: Attach the image-transform binding, so your Worker can resize and re-encode bytes it already holds. Defaults to `false`.

name.description: The identifier your Worker reads the key-value store through. Defaults to `KV`.

kv.description: The site's own key-value store. Declaring it provisions one namespace on the first publish and binds it.

bindings.description: What this bundle asks to be wired to.

cpuMs.description: CPU milliseconds per invocation. Defaults to 10000; the platform ceiling is 30000.

subRequests.description: Outbound sub-requests per invocation. Defaults to 20; the platform ceiling is 50.

limits.description: The caps this bundle asks for. The platform decides the ceilings and refuses anything over them.

compatibilityFlags.description: Workers compatibility flags your Worker needs to start — global_fetch_strictly_public, nodejs_compat. Anything else is refused by name. Set this only when your bundle ships no JSON Wrangler config for us to read it from.

compatibilityDate.description: The Workers compatibility date your bundle was COMPILED against, as `YYYY-MM-DD`. It is ignored unless it is newer than the platform's own pin — it can only move the date forward, never back.

runtime.description: What this bundle's Worker needs from the Workers runtime. Read from your bundle's own `wrangler.json` when it ships one; declare it here otherwise.

PagesDeployManifest.description: `pages.deploy.json` — the one file a bundle uses to say what it is and what it needs. Put it at the bundle root.
